title: Crack Infosys SP / DSE
subtitle: 12 steps from warm-up to the Hard slot — in the order you should learn them
description:
**What the test looks like (from candidate reports, not official):** in-person, proctored, ~3 hours. Traditionally **3 coding questions** (Easy / Medium / Hard, often weighted ~20/30/50); some recent drives reported **4** (easy, medium, hard, complex). Scoring is **partial — per test case passed**, so a correct brute force on the hard question still earns marks.

- **Q1** – arrays, strings, hashing, greedy
- **Q2** – greedy / sliding window / prefix sums / binary search
- **Q3+** – DP (most frequent), graphs, trees, bit manipulation, number theory, with `N` up to `10^5`

**Cutoff hints from reports:** ~1 full + 2 partial solutions often gets an interview call; solving all usually maps to SP, fewer to DSE. Python is allowed — but write efficient code (`sys.stdin`, avoid recursion depth issues, avoid O(N²) when `N = 10^5`).

**How to use this track:** go step by step. Inside each step, do problems in order. Give every problem 30–40 minutes before opening hints; open the editorial only after that; re-solve 'assisted' problems from scratch 3 days later.

steps.title: Warm-up: I/O, strings & counting
steps.goal: Get fast and error-free with stdin parsing, strings and frequency counting — the Q1 skill set.
tips: Read all input at once: `data = sys.stdin.read().split()`
Use `collections.Counter` and `dict.get(x, 0)` fluently
Always re-read the output format: YES/NO vs Yes/No, spaces vs newlines

steps.title: Hashing patterns
steps.goal: Turn O(N²) pair/group searches into O(N) with hash maps.
tips: Two-sum pattern: look up `target - x` before inserting `x`
A canonical key (sorted string, tuple of counts) groups equivalent items
Sort by a tuple key `(-count, value)` for deterministic tie-breaking

resources.title: Search YouTube: hashing patterns for coding interviews

steps.title: Prefix sums + hashing
steps.goal: Answer subarray questions in O(N) by remembering earlier prefix sums.
tips: sum(l..r) = P[r+1] - P[l]
Count subarrays with property → hashmap of prefix value → count
Longest subarray → hashmap of prefix value → FIRST index
Remainders: normalise with `% k` (Python already gives non-negative)

resources.title: Search YouTube: prefix sum + hashmap subarray problems

steps.title: Two pointers, sliding window & Kadane
steps.goal: Handle contiguous-window and pair problems in linear time.
tips: Sliding window works when expanding/shrinking changes the condition monotonically (e.g. positive numbers)
Kadane: best ending here = max(x, best_ending_prev + x)
Circular max = max(normal Kadane, total − min subarray) — careful when all are negative

steps.title: Greedy & sorting (Infosys Q1/Q2 favourites)
steps.goal: Recognise when a locally best choice is globally optimal — and prove it with an exchange argument.
tips: Interval scheduling: sort by END time
Platforms / meeting rooms: sort starts and ends separately and sweep
Custom order: `functools.cmp_to_key`
Monotonic stack for 'remove digits to make largest/smallest'

resources.title: Search YouTube: greedy algorithms interval scheduling

steps.title: Math, bits & modular arithmetic
steps.goal: Handle huge numbers with fast power, modular inverse, sieve and bit tricks.
tips: `pow(a, b, mod)` is built in; inverse mod prime p = `pow(a, p-2, p)`
Sieve once up to the max value, reuse for all queries
a + b = (a XOR b) + 2·(a AND b)

steps.title: Binary search on the answer & recursion
steps.goal: Convert 'minimise the maximum' into a yes/no check; enumerate small search spaces cleanly.
tips: If check(x) is monotonic, binary search x
Write `check` first, test it, then add the binary search
Backtracking: choose → recurse → un-choose; prune early

steps.title: Dynamic programming foundations
steps.goal: Master state → transition → base case → order, on the four classic DP families.
tips: Write the recursive brute force first, then memoise, then convert to a table
In Python prefer bottom-up loops (no recursion limit, faster)
LIS in O(N log N) uses `bisect`

resources.title: Search YouTube: Aditya Verma DP playlist

steps.title: Infosys-style DP — the Hard slot
steps.goal: Solve the DP problems that most often appear as Infosys Q3: counting mod 1e9+7, knapsack variants, partition/interval DP, DP on strings, digit DP.
tips: Counting answers → everything `% (10**9 + 7)` at every step
Partition into K segments: dp[k][i] = min over j of dp[k-1][j] + cost(j, i)
Interval DP: iterate by LENGTH of the interval
If stuck, code a brute force — partial marks count!

resources.title: Search YouTube: Infosys SP DSE DP questions

steps.title: Graphs
steps.goal: BFS/DFS, multi-source BFS, DSU, topological sort and Dijkstra (including state-expanded Dijkstra).
tips: Use `collections.deque` for BFS, `heapq` for Dijkstra
Never use recursive DFS for N = 10^5 in Python — use an explicit stack
Extra constraint (k passes, parity…) → put it in the state: (node, k)

steps.title: Trees & range queries
steps.goal: Flatten trees with an Euler tour and answer subtree/path queries with a Fenwick tree.
tips: Euler tour: subtree of v = contiguous range [tin[v], tout[v]]
Fenwick tree: point update + prefix sum in O(log N), ~10 lines of code
Count inversions with a Fenwick tree over compressed values

steps.title: Advanced mix: strings, combinatorics, XOR, stacks
steps.goal: The 'complex' question: combine two techniques under tight constraints.
tips: Prefix function (KMP) answers border/period/palindrome-prefix questions in O(N)
nCr mod p: precompute factorials and inverse factorials once
XOR basis: rank r of N numbers → 2^(N−r) subsets XOR to any reachable value
Count 'bad' and subtract from total when 'good' is hard to count
